notes: "Why does Standish not come?" is a little stiff; "Why doesn't Standish come?" sounds more natural (taste, not a failure).
"So John said, 'Yes, I can go.'" reads slightly textbook-like; "Yes, I will go" or "All right, I will go" is more natural, though 'can' is understandable.

"Why don't you speak for yourself, John?" is idiomatic, but it is the famous key line, it is quiz-tested, and the context (John praising Standish) makes the meaning clear enough. Optionally, add one sentence after it, e.g. "She wanted John, not the captain."
Quiz Q3 distractor "the captain of the Mayflower" is close to Standish's title ("captain of Plymouth"). The keyed answer is still unambiguous.
"Why does the captain not come to me himself?" is slightly formal, but it suits the period voice.
The step from the false death news to the wedding ("Soon John and Priscilla had their wedding.") is abrupt, but it is logically clear.
Grammar stays within B1: no conditionals and no passive. The 'would sail' future-in-the-past and the relative clause are acceptable at B1.

It is faithful to the poem: Standish reading, John writing letters for the Mayflower, the mayflowers, the spinning wheel and hymn, the accusation about roof and table, the council messenger, the dawn departure, the false report of death, the reappearance at the wedding, the remark about doing one's own asking, and the white bull led by the nose-ring.
The prose is genuinely literary rather than padded. "neither of them was entirely deceived by the word" is a nice touch.
The death is only reported, and the burials are euphemistic ("laid to rest"). This fits a 4+ rating.

summary: All five levels faithfully retell Longfellow's poem in the right order with the correct ending. Each level is consistent with the others and appropriate for a 4+ rating, with deaths only stated. Grammar and vocabulary fit each CEFR band, and every quiz has a single defensible keyed answer. Only minor stylistic notes remain, mainly two slightly stiff A1/A2 question forms.
